theme: True fasting; the LORD returns; nations included
readingInstruction: Read Zechariah 7:1-8:23. A delegation asks whether they should keep a fast, and Zechariah answers with a question about justice and mercy. Then come eight promises of restoration. Read the final verses of chapter 8.
settingTheScene: Two years after the visions, in 518 BC, a delegation from Bethel asks the priests whether they should continue to mourn and fast in the fifth month, the month the temple was destroyed. Zechariah answers in two parts: first a rebuke about the heart behind religious practice, and then a series of promises. This is the point where the book turns from visions to messages.
observation: “When you fasted and mourned… was it for me that you fasted?” (7:5).
“Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy to one another” (7:9).
“Do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor, and let none of you devise evil against another in your heart” (7:10).
“They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law” (7:12).
“I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy” (8:2).
“I will return to Zion and dwell in the midst of Jerusalem” (8:3).
“Old men and old women shall again sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each with his staff in his hand because of great age. And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing” (8:4-5).
“In those days ten men from the nations of every tongue shall take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying, Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you” (8:23).
interpretation:
The question is about a fast. For seventy years the exiles had fasted in the fifth and seventh months to remember the destruction. Now that the temple is being rebuilt, should they continue? Zechariah first asks a hard question: “Was it for me that you fasted? And when you eat and drink, do you not eat and drink for yourselves?” Their religion had become self-focused. They were going through the motions.

Then he reminds them of the former prophets, who said the same thing: “Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy to one another. Do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor.” The ancestors would not listen. “They made their hearts diamond-hard.” Justice and mercy were the point. The exile resulted from ignoring them. The people of the return must learn from this.

Then chapter 8 brings ten promises, each beginning, “Thus says the LORD of hosts.” God is jealous for Zion. He will return and dwell in Jerusalem, which will be called the “faithful city.” The picture is of an ordinary, peaceful city: old men and women sitting in the streets, boys and girls playing. It is one of the loveliest images in the prophets. God’s salvation is not only grand but domestic, a place safe for the old and the young.

The people are told: “Let your hands be strong.” And God promises that their fasts will become “joy and gladness and cheerful feasts.” The fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months, all memories of Jerusalem’s fall, will be turned into feasts. Sorrow will be transformed. The chapter ends with a vision of the nations: ten men take hold of a Jew’s robe and say, “Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.” The mission of Israel to the nations is fulfilled in the church.
connection: Isaiah 58:3-7 describes the fast God desires. Matthew 6:16-18 speaks of fasting before the Father. Matthew 23:23: justice, mercy, and faithfulness are the weightier matters of the law. Micah 6:8: do justice, love kindness, walk humbly. James 1:27: religion that is pure is to visit orphans and widows in their affliction. Luke 5:34-35: when the bridegroom is with us, there is no mourning. Revelation 21:4.
application:
Ask whether any spiritual practice in your life has become a ritual done for yourself. Reshape it around love for God and neighbor.

Show “kindness and mercy” to a widow, an orphan, a foreigner, or a poor person this week.

Pray for the day when old men and women sit in the streets and children play, and work for the safety of such a place.
prayerPrompts: Confess where your religion has been for yourself.
Ask him to teach you to render true judgments and show mercy.
Ask him to make you glad in him.
